title: Brookside Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Brookside wells have a 50 ft median depth, but fractured bedrock can push drilling to 2,200 ft.
intro_html:
Brookside sits in mountain terrain where well conditions can change quickly from parcel to parcel. Within 5 miles, Colorado Division of Water Resources records include 1,426 permitted wells. Most reported wells are shallow, but the deepest recorded well reaches 2,200 feet, reflecting the uncertainty of fractured granite and gneiss.

This page uses permitted-well records around Brookside, including nearby Lincoln Park, Williamsburg, Cañon City, Rockvale, Park Center and Florence. Use the statistics to screen a property, not to guarantee its result. A driller still needs to evaluate the specific lot, access, geology, casing and water-rights requirements.

sections.heading: Brookside well depth depends on the bedrock
sections.html:
The median reported well depth near Brookside is 50 feet. The middle half of wells falls from 32 to 77 feet, and 80% are under 100 feet. That is a useful starting point for a drilling conversation, but it does not make a shallow bid certain.

Depth becomes less predictable in the fractured-bedrock setting. The 90th-percentile depth is 250 feet, while the deepest record is 2,200 feet. About 11% of wells are from 100 to 300 feet, 6% from 300 to 600 feet, and 3% exceed 600 feet. Ask for a bid that explains the per-foot rate and what happens if the hole must continue past the expected formation.

sections.heading: What Brookside wells produce
sections.html:
Among the wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute. The middle half produces from 4.8 to 15.0 gallons per minute. The spread matters more than the median when planning a home, livestock use or irrigation.

  • 3% report less than 1 gallon per minute.
  • 23% report from 1 to 5 gallons per minute.
  • 43% report from 5 to 15 gallons per minute.
  • 31% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 189 wells report a pump yield, so nearby records are a screening tool rather than a guarantee. A low-yield well may still work with storage, while a buyer should confirm the permitted use and any pumping limitations before relying on the result.

sections.heading: Brookside water levels and the available trend
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 24 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 22 to 80 feet. Only 30 wells report a static water level, so this is a limited sample and may not represent every part of Brookside.

The decade figures show a deeper median reported water level in the available records: 22 feet in the 2010s and 37 feet in the 2020s. That difference suggests water was measured farther below the surface in the newer decade, but it does not by itself prove a basin-wide declining water table. Well location, construction, season and measurement conditions can all affect the comparison. Have a driller evaluate the lot and ask whether a current water-level measurement is available.

sections.heading: Who has drilled around Brookside, and when
sections.html:
Permit records show activity across several decades, with the largest recorded issuance period in the 1990s at 381 permits. The record also includes 235 permits from the 2000s, 158 from the 2010s and 96 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025, so Brookside continues to have recent well activity.

The most active names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 485 wells, Arkansas Valley Drilling (Moore, Todd A.) with 72, and Young'S Drilling & Pump Serv (Young, Nolen) with 64. These records identify drilling history, not a recommendation or guarantee of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scope, access needs and the proposed construction method directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Brookside drilling cost in fractured mountain ground
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock, described as granite and gneiss. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $3,200 to $5,000. That is the hole only, not a complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $9,200 to $17,000 at the median depth. A deeper-than-typical hole can move the price substantially, and fractured rock can produce an unexpected result even after drilling. Get the written estimate separated into drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, storage, trenching, electrical and testing so competing bids can be compared fairly.

sections.heading: Brookside risks to check before construction
sections.html:
Low yield is not the only concern. The records identify 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 95 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those mapped locations do not prove that a particular parcel is contaminated, but they are a reason to check the property history, nearby land uses and available water-quality information.

Most permitted wells are identified with an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer: 1,378 wells. The records include 18 alluvial wells and 7 Dakota Sandstone wells, with no Denver Basin aquifer wells. Before buying, ask for a water test and confirm well construction, casing, grout and septic separation. A low-yield or dry hole can also affect a building plan, so verify access for a rig and space for the septic system before closing.

sections.heading: Buying or building a lot near Brookside
sections.html:
Start with the exact parcel, then review nearby permits rather than relying on the area median. Lincoln Park is about 1 mile away, Williamsburg about 2 miles, Cañon City about 3 miles, Rockvale about 4 miles, and Park Center and Florence about 5 miles. Their records can provide context, but geology may change across short distances.

For an existing home, obtain the well permit, construction report, pump information, recent production evidence and water-quality results. For vacant land, have a licensed driller assess access, likely depth, yield risk and the best well location before you finalize a house or septic design. Check Colorado DWR requirements and the permitted use; household-use wells are commonly exempt wells, but an augmentation plan may be required in an over-appropriated basin. Put testing and well contingencies in the purchase contract.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Brookside, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Brookside is 50 feet, and the middle half runs from 32 to 77 feet. About 80% are under 100 feet. Conditions vary sharply in fractured granite and gneiss: the 90th-percentile depth is 250 feet, and the deepest record is 2,200 feet.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Brookside?
faq.a: The local model uses $65 to $100 per foot in fractured mountain bedrock. At the 50-foot median depth, the drilled hole is about $3,200 to $5,000. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $9,200 to $17,000. Deeper drilling or difficult access can change the bid.

faq.q: How much water do Brookside wells produce?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 4.8 to 15.0 gallons per minute. About 3% report under 1 gallon per minute, while 31% report more than 15 gallons per minute. Only 189 wells report yield, so nearby records cannot promise a particular lot's production.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Brookside, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety cannot be determined from depth or yield alone. Within about 10 miles, records identify 33 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 95 historic mine features and 5 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the actual well, review nearby land uses and ask for construction records before relying on the water for a home.

faq.q: Are Brookside well water levels dropping?
faq.a: The available records show a median static water level of 22 feet below surface in the 2010s and 37 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported level in the newer decade, but only 30 wells report static water levels. The comparison suggests a possible change, not proof of a basin-wide decline.
